pick.headline: Shcharansky freed in Glienicke Bridge spy swap
pick.summary: On February 11, 1986, Soviet dissident Anatoly Shcharansky walked across the Glienicke Bridge between West Berlin and Potsdam, freed in an exchange that also traded several Western-held Eastern bloc agents for people held in the East.
pick.significance: Moscow had convicted Shcharansky of spying for the CIA, a charge Washington denied. The swap was the most celebrated exchange on the 'bridge of spies'.
pick.fbis: The Soviet Union Daily Report of February 11, 1986, carried Hamburg DPA's account of the East-West "agent" exchange on Berlin's Glienicke Bridge: Shcharanskiy handed over and driven off in the U.S. ambassador's car, alongside the Koechers, Zemlyakov and others traded by the West.

alternates.headline: Iranian army declares neutrality; revolution triumphs
alternates.summary: On February 11, 1979, Iran's military declared itself neutral, Prime Minister Shapur Bakhtiar's government fell and revolutionaries took control of Tehran.
alternates.significance: The date is marked in Iran as the victory of the Islamic Revolution. The new regime soon turned against the United States.
alternates.fbis: The Soviet Union Daily Report of February 12, 1979, carried Moscow World Service in English on February 11: Iran's Supreme Military Council declared neutrality and sent troops to barracks, and Tehran was then "practically in the hands of the insurgents", who seized the government residence and television station.

alternates.headline: Nelson Mandela freed
alternates.summary: On February 11, 1990, Nelson Mandela walked out of Victor Verster prison after 27 years in custody.
alternates.significance: His release launched the negotiations that ended apartheid.
alternates.fbis: The East Europe Daily Report of February 12, 1990, carried East Berlin ADN: the GDR Foreign Ministry welcomed Mandela's release "with deep satisfaction" as a strong impulse toward democratic change in South Africa, and floated future relations with a changed South Africa.
